cls: Antipsychotic (substituted benzamide; selective D2/D3 dopamine antagonist)
pharm: Selective dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist with bimodal dose-dependent activity (alerting/antidepressant at low dose, antipsychotic at high dose)
quick: Positive symptoms: start 400 mg PO twice daily, up to 1200 mg twice daily; negative symptoms: 200-400 mg twice daily
May be taken with or without food; avoid late-evening dosing due to alerting effect
Not recommended unless clearly necessary; monitor neonate for extrapyramidal/withdrawal signs
Excreted in breast milk in relatively large amounts; breastfeeding not recommended
Reduce dose or extend interval; sulpiride is largely renally excreted
No specific adjustment needed (minimal hepatic metabolism)
ECG/QT, electrolytes, prolactin, EPS, weight, blood counts
summary: Sulpiride is a substituted benzamide antipsychotic that selectively antagonises dopamine D2/D3 receptors. It is used for acute and chronic schizophrenia and shows bimodal, dose-dependent activity: lower doses have an alerting and antidepressant effect on negative/depressive symptoms, while higher doses control positive psychotic symptoms. It is largely excreted unchanged by the kidneys, so doses must be reduced in renal impairment. Key risks include hyperprolactinaemia, extrapyramidal symptoms, dose-dependent QT prolongation, tardive dyskinesia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
indications: Treatment of acute and chronic schizophrenia (positive and negative symptoms)
Low-dose use for predominantly negative symptoms and associated depressive/withdrawn presentations (per benzamide bimodal activity)

dosage.d: Start at least 400 mg twice daily; increase if necessary up to a suggested maximum of 1200 mg twice daily
dosage.t: Two divided doses (morning and early evening)
dosage.n: Increasing above 1200 mg twice daily has not been shown to give further improvement

dosage.d: Start 400 mg twice daily; reducing towards 200 mg twice daily increases the alerting effect
dosage.n: Negative symptoms generally respond to doses below 800 mg daily
Titrate to balance positive and negative symptom control

dosage.d: Same dose ranges apply; reduce dose if there is evidence of renal impairment
dosage.n: Increased susceptibility to EPS, sedation, and postural hypotension

dosage.d: Reduce dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval according to severity of impairment
dosage.n: Sulpiride is excreted largely unchanged in urine

admin: Swallow tablets/solution as prescribed in two divided daily doses
Avoid administering the second dose late in the evening because of the alerting effect
Obtain a baseline ECG and electrolytes before treatment in patients with cardiac risk factors
Titrate gradually and use the lowest effective dose, particularly in the elderly and renal impairment
Do not co-administer with levodopa or other dopaminergic antiparkinsonian agents
moa: Sulpiride is a substituted benzamide that selectively blocks dopamine D2 and D3 receptors with relatively little affinity for other receptor types. It shows bimodal, dose-related activity: at low doses presynaptic dopamine autoreceptor blockade predominates, producing an alerting and antidepressant effect on negative and depressive symptoms, whereas at higher doses postsynaptic blockade in mesolimbic pathways controls positive psychotic symptoms. Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade increases prolactin secretion.

absolute: Concurrent levodopa or other dopaminergic antiparkinsonian drugs
relative: Cardiovascular disease, bradycardia, congenital or acquired QT prolongation, electrolyte disturbance
Elderly with dementia (increased mortality with antipsychotics)
Risk factors for venous thromboembolism or stroke
monitor: Full blood count for signs of dyscrasia

preg: There are inadequate data on the use of sulpiride in pregnant women. Sulpiride crosses the placenta. Neonates exposed in the third trimester are at risk of extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, feeding/respiratory difficulty). Use during pregnancy only if clearly necessary, and monitor the neonate accordingly.
lact: Sulpiride is excreted into breast milk in relatively large amounts. Because of insufficient data on infant safety, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment.
renal: Sulpiride is excreted largely unchanged by the kidneys (around 95% of the compound is eliminated unchanged in urine and faeces). In renal impairment the dose should be reduced and/or the dosing interval lengthened in proportion to the degree of impairment. Reduce the dose in the elderly where renal function may be decreased.
hepatic: Sulpiride undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, so no specific dose adjustment is generally required for hepatic impairment. Use clinical judgement and the lowest effective dose.

major: Levodopa and dopaminergic antiparkinsonian agents (mutual antagonism - contraindicated)
Other QT-prolonging drugs such as class IA/III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol), methadone, certain antipsychotics and antimicrobials (additive torsades risk)
Drugs causing bradycardia or hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia (increase torsades de pointes risk)
moderate: CNS depressants, opioids, benzodiazepines, antihistamines, anaesthetics (additive sedation)
Lithium (increased risk of neurotoxicity and EPS)
Antacids and sucralfate (reduce sulpiride absorption - separate dosing by at least 2 hours)
minor: Other dopamine antagonists (additive prolactin elevation and EPS)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; separate from antacids/sucralfate by at least 2 hours to avoid reduced absorption
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; it enhances the sedative effect of sulpiride
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum prolactin and may produce false-positive pregnancy tests; can interfere with interpretation of prolactin-related investigations

serious: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
rare: Hyponatraemia / syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness, raised creatine kinase) - discontinue immediately and provide emergency supportive care
Syncope, palpitations, or arrhythmia suggesting torsades de pointes - urgent ECG and correction of electrolytes

monitoring: ECG / QT interval at baseline and with dose changes in at-risk patients
Serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium), correcting deficits before/during therapy
Serum prolactin, especially with symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia
Extrapyramidal symptoms and signs of tardive dyskinesia
Body weight, fasting glucose and lipids
Full blood count if signs of infection or unexplained fever
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed; do not stop abruptly without medical advice
Avoid the evening dose late at night as the medicine can be alerting
Report fever with muscle stiffness, palpitations, fainting, or unusual movements promptly
Be aware of possible breast changes, milk production, or menstrual/sexual changes from raised prolactin
Avoid alcohol and activities needing alertness until you know how the drug affects you
Tell your doctor about kidney problems and any heart-rhythm conditions
pk: Mood elevation may appear within a few days; antipsychotic effect develops over days to weeks
Peak plasma concentration about 3-6 hours after an oral dose
Consistent with twice-daily dosing; effect sustained over the dosing interval
Store in original packaging below 25 C; protect from moisture (follow product label)
pearls: Not FDA-approved; this information is derived from EMA/UK SmPC and BNF/manufacturer prescribing sources (e.g., Dolmatil, Sulpor)
Bimodal dosing: lower doses target negative/depressive symptoms, higher doses target positive symptoms
Largely renally cleared - reduce dose in renal impairment and the elderly
Strong association with hyperprolactinaemia compared with many other antipsychotics
Contraindicated with levodopa and in prolactin-dependent tumours and phaeochromocytoma
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not take a double dose, and avoid taking a dose so late that it disturbs sleep.
overdose: Experience is limited; doses up to about 16 g have been reported without fatality. Features may include drowsiness, extrapyramidal reactions (dystonia, torticollis), agitation, and dose-dependent QT prolongation with risk of arrhythmia. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with cardiac/ECG monitoring, correction of electrolytes, and anticholinergic agents for severe dystonic reactions. Sulpiride is only poorly removed by dialysis. Contact a poison control centre.
